one_liner: Header-only C++20 binary BVH builder and ray traverser; its chart shows it faster than nanort and Fast-BVH, but slower than Embree.
what_it_does: Builds a bounding volume hierarchy over any primitives for which you supply bounding boxes and centers, and traverses it with rays or a custom top-down visitor. The high-level DefaultBuilder picks a builder from a Low, Medium or High quality setting and an optional ThreadPool. The low-level API exposes each builder (sweep SAH, binned SAH, mini-tree), a reinsertion optimizer, refit, subtree extraction and serialization. Ray-triangle and ray-sphere intersection, any-hit traversal and a C API are included. You get raw index ranges into a prim_ids array and write the leaf intersection lambda yourself, so it is a toolkit rather than a drop-in replacement for nanort's or Embree's API.
how_it_is_fast: Low quality uses Wald's binned SAH builder. Medium and High use a full sweep SAH builder single-threaded, or, with a thread pool and at least 1,024 primitives, Ganestam et al.'s mini-tree builder with pruning. High then runs Meister and Bittner's parallel reinsertion optimizer to raise tree quality. Nodes are compact binary nodes with siblings stored next to each other and one packed index (first child or primitive plus primitive count). Traversal visits the nearer child first and orders box tests by ray octant, uses FMA-based slab tests (Ize's robust variant is optional) and a fixed-size stack; shadow rays can use SATO ordering.
when_to_use: CPU ray tracers, path tracers or visibility queries that need a small dependency-free BVH (standard library only), and where Embree's size or license model is unwanted.
Replacing nanort or Fast-BVH: the README chart shows faster build and roughly 2-4x faster primary-ray render than both.
Choosing your own trade-off between build time and traversal quality per scene (Low, Medium, High), for example a quick rebuild for animated geometry and High for static scenes.
Non-ray queries on a BVH (box overlap, custom culling, 2D or 4D bounding boxes, float or double), using traverse_top_down with your own inner-node and leaf callbacks.
C projects that only need the high-level build and intersect functions, through the optional C API (BVH_BUILD_C_API).
when_not_to_use: Peak performance: Embree 3.13 beats every preset on the README chart (about 70 ms build and 170 ms render, against about 150 ms and 275 ms for v2 medium), and TinyBVH reports beating both.
Packet or wide-BVH (BVH4 or BVH8) SIMD traversal and GPU traversal: the nodes are binary and the traversal is single-ray (the GPU question is issue #92).
Toolchains without C++20 (it uses std::span and defaulted comparison operators) or with CMake older than 3.21.
Packaging that needs versioned releases: there is no tagged v2 release, and issue #116 asks for one for Debian.
Frequent incremental insert or remove: there is refit but no dynamic insertion, so topology changes mean a rebuild (asked in issues #94 and #85).

integration.dependencies: none beyond the C++ standard library (Threads::Threads linked for the std::thread-based pool); optional C API library
integration.platforms: any (portable C++; GCC, Clang and MSVC force-inline macros in platform.h)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. A built Bvh is plain std::vector data and intersect() is const with a caller-owned stack, so concurrent read-only traversal with one stack per thread looks safe from the source. Builders take a ThreadPool that defaults to std::thread::hardware_concurrency() threads.

gotchas: SmallStack<Index, N> (the benchmark uses N = 64) checks overflow only with assert(), so a BVH deeper than N overflows silently in release builds. Issue #108 (December 2025) asks what depth is safe and has no visible answer; use GrowingStack or size the stack to the tree depth.
Leaves hold ranges into bvh.prim_ids, not your primitive order. Either index through prim_ids or permute your primitives after building, which the benchmark's --permute_prims option does.

The README is out of date in places: it says -DENABLE_TESTING=ON and -DBVH_STATIC_LINK_STDLIB_C_API=ON, but CMakeLists uses CTest's BUILD_TESTING and BVH_C_API_STATIC_LINK_STDLIB, and the snippet's target_link_library should be target_link_libraries.

Past bugs fixed upstream: ReinsertionOptimizer could loop forever (#84), extract_bvh could use a stale pointer (#81), and a span went out of range below 3 dimensions (#106). Pin a commit that includes these fixes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: TinyBVH is the closer competitor and claims to beat both Embree and this library on build time, so prefer it for top speed or wide BVHs. Pick madmann91/bvh for a clean, modern-C++ API with multiple builders, arbitrary dimensions and scalar types, serialization and a C API. ArborX and Coal are for spatial queries and collision on a different scale.
verified_claims_summary: One README chart (chart.png) compares build time and 1-spp 720p primary-ray render time on one unnamed .obj scene. Readings, approximate: v2 medium about 150 ms build and 275 ms render; nanort about 360 and 645; Fast-BVH about 460 and 1225; Embree 3.13 about 70 and 170. That makes v2 roughly 2.3x faster than nanort and 4.5x faster than Fast-BVH at rendering (derived from page data), but slower than Embree. No CPU, compiler, flags, thread count or scene is given. test/benchmark.cpp times only this library: it builds with a thread pool sized to hardware_concurrency and renders single-threaded. The harness used for Embree, nanort and Fast-BVH is not in the repo.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-21, 1.2k stars, 438 commits) and MIT-licensed. It is header-only and easy to vendor, but has no tagged v2 release, so pin a commit.
